RockShiny — Implementation Guide

The complete reference: every module, every design decision, every measurement.

New here? Start with the short GUIDE.md: what the app does, how to run it, and where things are, in ten minutes. Come back here for the details.

RockShiny is a Shiny app that opens Rocksmith 2014 .psarc files (and Standard MIDI files) and plays them on a Rocksmith-style 3-D note highway, with the song audio in sync, on guitar/bass, piano or harmonica.

A second mode, karaoke, shows the lyrics of songs that have them, highlighted syllable by syllable in time with the audio, in the app or as a standalone HTML page (Step 13).

1. Architecture

R does file I/O, decryption, decompression and data wrangling, once per song. The browser does everything that runs per frame. Nothing that needs precise timing goes through the R websocket.

How RockShiny works

Detailed flow

 ┌──────────────────────────── R (Shiny server) ─────────────────────────────┐
 │ mod_import ──► load_song() ──► psarc_open()  AES-CFB TOC, zlib blocks      │
 │                     │                                                      │
 │                     ├─► song_chart() ─► parse_arrangement_xml()  (CDLC)    │
 │                     │                 └► parse_arrangement_sng() (official)│
 │                     │                 └► build_chart()  DD merge, chords   │
 │                     │                 └► chart_for_instrument() piano/harp │
 │                     │                 └► chart_json()   column JSON ───────┼──► output value (once)
 │ .mid ─► read_midi() ─► midi_parts() ─► (same chart path, no audio)         │
 │                     └─► song_audio() ─► find_song_wem() (.bnk lookup)      │
 │                                        convert_wem() vgmstream → ffmpeg    │
 │                                        cache/<md5>/audio.ogg ─────────────┼──► static URL (httpuv)
 │ mod_karaoke ─► load_karaoke_song() ─► song_vocals_raw() + manifest + art   │
 │                     └─► karaoke_json()  lyrics columns ────────────────────┼──► output value (once)
 │                     └─► audio_feed()    same cache + background jobs ──────┼──► static URL (httpuv)
 │                     └─► karaoke_export_html()  standalone page (HTML) ─────┼──► .html file
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 ┌──────────────────────────── Browser ──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ binding.js   Shiny output binding + controller (transport, keys, loop)     │
 │ clock.js     <audio> is the master clock, extrapolated per frame          │
 │ renderer.js  Canvas 2D + hand-rolled perspective camera, draw(t)           │
 │ renderer-lanes.js  piano keyboard / harmonica lanes (same camera + clock)  │
 │ guide.js     guide tones: the chart on a Web Audio synth, latency-aligned  │
 │  requestAnimationFrame ─► clock.tick(ts) ─► renderer.draw(t - offset)       │
 │ mic.js       getUserMedia ─► AudioWorklet (pitch-worklet.js: onsets +      │
 │              spectra) ─► NoteVerifier ─► input.js HitJudge ─► renderers    │
 │ karaoke.js   lyrics: timing model + DOM view, on clock.js (same sync);     │
 │              hosts: karaoke-shiny.js (Shiny) / karaoke-page.js (HTML page) │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Channels between R and the browser

Channel Direction When Payload
output value (renderHighway) R → JS once per arrangement chart JSON (40–70 KB typical, ~290 KB for a 7,400-note rhythm chart)
custom message rs-highway R → JS rarely audio (head/full), settings, play/pause/seek, status, input, benchmark, calibrate, result_ack
input <id>_ready JS → R after each chart load {songKey, audio: none/head/full, formats} (starts the audio job)
input <id>_state JS → R 4 Hz while playing {t, playing, section, sectionIndex, rate, loops, fps}
input <id>_section_pick JS → R double-click on a timeline section {index} → practice pickers + loop on
input <id>_loop_toggle JS → R L key / loop badge flips the “Loop this part” switch
input <id>_benchmark JS → R after “Benchmark renderers” per-renderer fps / frame-time results
input <id>_judge JS → R ≤ 2.5 Hz while an input source is on {hits, misses, perfect, streak, bestStreak, accuracy, score, multiplier}
input <id>_result JS → R end of a scored song / each loop pass {kind: song/loop, accuracy, score, sections, coverage, rate, ...} → scores.csv
input <id>_devices / _input_status / _calibration JS → R microphone start / calibration input devices, start errors, measured input latency
input <id>_latency JS → R on Play / device change {outputMs, routed, auto}
output value (renderKaraoke) R → JS once per karaoke song karaoke JSON (~50 KB: lyrics, sections, album art)
custom message rs-karaoke R → JS rarely audio (head/full), settings, play/pause/seek, status
input <id>_ready / <id>_latency (karaoke) JS → R after each song load / on Play as for the highway (starts the audio job; latency info)

3. Setup

R packages

# xml2 and openssl are new relative to renv.lock
renv::install(c("xml2", "openssl"))
renv::snapshot()
shiny::runApp()

External tools (audio only)

Without them the highway and karaoke still work, silently.

Tool Why Install
vgmstream-cli decodes Wwise Vorbis .wem → WAV macOS brew install vgmstream; Windows/Linux: release zip from https://vgmstream.org
ffmpeg WAV → OGG Vorbis (or AAC) brew install ffmpeg / https://ffmpeg.org

If a tool isn’t on PATH, point to it:

options(rockshiny.vgmstream = "/path/vgmstream-cli", rockshiny.ffmpeg = "/path/ffmpeg")

Options

Option Default What it does
rockshiny.cache_dir tools::R_user_dir("RockShiny", "cache") converted audio; persistent
rockshiny.audio_format "auto" or "ogg", "m4a", "opus", "flac", "wav": try that format first
rockshiny.library_dir "songs" the songs folder (.psarc and .mid; the bundled inst/examples demo is always listed too)
rockshiny.prewarm TRUE FALSE: no background pre-decoding of the library
rockshiny.head_seconds 30 length of the quick-start clip
rockshiny.data_dir tools::R_user_dir("RockShiny", "data") where scores.csv (scored runs) is kept

Console use (no Shiny involved)

song  <- load_song("songs/Pink-Floyd_Wish-You-Were-Here_v5_DD_m.psarc")
song                                   # arrangements table
chart <- song_chart(song, "wishyouwhizzhere_lead")
head(chart$notes)                      # time, string, fret, sustain, slide_to, bend, tech, chord
song_audio(song)                       # path to cached audio.ogg

k <- load_karaoke_song("songs/Dire-Straits_Sultans-of-Swing_v443_m.psarc")
karaoke_lines(k)                       # one string per lyric line
karaoke_export_html(k, "sultans.html") # standalone karaoke page

Without R: Python

tools/karaoke_export_html.py writes the same karaoke pages as karaoke_export_html() (byte-identical output, see Step 13). It needs Python 3.9+ and pip install cryptography; for audio, vgmstream-cli on PATH or pip install wem2ogg, plus ffmpeg.

python3 tools/karaoke_export_html.py songs/Dire-Straits_Sultans-of-Swing_v443_m.psarc -o sultans.html
python3 tools/karaoke_export_html.py --library songs -o songbook.html --audio files


4. Step by step


Step 1 · PSARC container

Files: R/psarc.R, R/crypto.R

In one line: open the archive, decrypt its table of contents, read any file inside.

  1. Header (32 bytes, big-endian): "PSAR", version, "zlib", toc_length (header + TOC), entry size (30), entry count, block size (65536), flags.
  2. TOC decryption: if flags & 4, the TOC is AES-256-CFB128 encrypted with a fixed key and IV. openssl has no CFB mode, so aes_cfb128_decrypt() builds it from single-block encryptions (CFB only needs the forward cipher). Verified against the NIST SP 800-38A vectors.
  3. Entries: md5[16] | zindex u32 | length u40 | offset u40. The 40-bit fields are decoded column-wise from a raw matrix (be_uint_cols()).
  4. Block table: the rest of the TOC holds one u16 per 64 KiB block.
    • 0 means a full block stored raw.
    • Otherwise the block is zlib, or stored raw when compression didn’t help (inflate_or_raw() checks the zlib header and falls back).
  5. Entry 0 is a newline-separated list naming entries 1..n. Each TOC md5 is md5(file name); the tests use that as an end-to-end check of decryption.
  6. Big entries (.wem, 15–65 MB) are streamed block by block to disk (psarc_read(arc, name, out = path)), never held whole in memory.


Step 2 · Arrangements and the right audio file

Files: R/song.R, R/audio.R

In one line: list the playable parts from the manifests, and find the full-song audio (not the preview).

  • Arrangements come from manifests/**/*.json (ArrangementName, song metadata). Vocals and ShowLights are skipped. Each manifest maps to songs/arr/<base>.xml and songs/bin/<platform>/<base>.sng.
  • Two .wem files per archive: the full song and the preview. The song soundbank (song_<key>.bnk, not _preview.bnk) contains its wem ID as a little-endian u32, so find_song_wem() searches the bank bytes (grepRaw).

Don’t use manifest order: in Sultans of Swing the preview is listed first.


Step 3 · Note charts

Files: R/arrangement_xml.R, R/sng.R

In one line: two independent parsers (XML and the compiled SNG) produce the same raw chart.

XML — present in CDLC built with the Custom Song Toolkit

  • Read only /song/levels/level/.... <transcriptionTrack> also contains <notes>/<chords>.
  • Dynamic Difficulty: DD files have one <level> per difficulty (up to 14 in the samples). The full chart is assembled per phrase iteration [start_i, start_{i+1}) using the level equal to that phrase’s maxDifficulty (select_max_difficulty(), a vectorised findInterval).
  • Chords: the chord template decides which strings and frets sound. <chordNote> children are often partial (for example, only the one muted string). They override per-string sustain, slide, bend and techniques but do not define the chord.

Treating <chordNote> children as the full chord silently loses notes: on 13 of the first 25 sample arrangements it dropped 2–58 % of all notes.

SNG — the compiled format; official DLC ships only this

  • u32 magic | u32 flags | IV[16] | AES-256-CTR payload. The payload is u32 length | zlib. The key depends on platform (songs/bin/macos/ vs generic/); "auto" tries both.
  • The body is a sequence of u32 count + packed struct arrays. Fixed-size arrays are skipped or decoded vectorised from their offsets. Only notes (trailing variable-length bend data) need a pointer walk.
  • Notes with chordId >= 0 are expanded through the chord template and the per-string chordNotes masks, then go through the same build_chart().

Cross-validation

XML and SNG are independent encodings of the same chart. On all 51 guitar/bass arrangements of the 18-song library (10 of them with Dynamic Difficulty), both paths agree note for note: time, string and fret, all 16 technique bits, slides, chord counts, anchors and beats.

The one difference is sustain on a chord whose strings have different sustains: the SNG stores one sustain per chord, so XML is preferred when present.


Step 4 · Chart model and JSON contract

Files: R/chart.R

In one line: the chart goes to the browser once, as columns that become typed arrays.

chart_json() sends columns, not rows. Each column becomes a typed array in JS (Float64Array times, Int8Array strings/frets). 1-element columns stay arrays (auto_unbox = FALSE, scalars unboxed explicitly):

{ "format": "rockshiny-chart/1", "songKey": "<md5>",
  "meta":  {"title": "...", "arrangement": "Lead", "n_strings": 6, "tuning": [0,0,0,0,0,0], ...},
  "notes": {"t": [], "s": [], "f": [], "sus": [], "tech": [], "slide": [], "slideU": [], "bend": [], "chord": []},
  "chords": {"t": [], "name": [], "hd": []},
  "anchors": {"t": [], "fret": [], "width": []},
  "beats": {"t": [], "m": []},
  "sections": {"t": [], "name": []} }

tech is a bit field that must be identical in R/chart.R and renderer.js:

bit technique bit technique
1 hammer-on 512 link-next
2 pull-off 1024 tap
4 palm mute 2048 bend
8 fret-hand mute 4096 slide
16 harmonic 8192 unpitched slide
32 pinch harmonic 16384 chord
64 vibrato 32768 ignore
128 tremolo
256 accent


Step 5 · Audio

Files: R/audio.R, R/audio_jobs.R, inst/bin/rs-convert.sh

In one line: decode the Wwise audio once per song, in the background, into a format this browser plays.

Pipeline

FFmpeg cannot decode Rocksmith audio. A .wem is a RIFF file with format tag 0xFFFF (Wwise Vorbis: headerless packets plus external codebooks). ffmpeg -i song.wem fails with “no decoder found”. This was confirmed on the sample files.

vgmstream-cli song.wem → wav (decoded once), then FFmpeg encodes a delivery format. The fallback decoder is ww2ogg with the codebook file, then revorb.

Format negotiation

FFmpeg builds differ: libvorbis, libopus and libmp3lame are optional external libraries, and some Homebrew/conda builds lack them, failing with “Unknown encoder ‘libvorbis’”. Browsers differ too: open-source Chromium has no AAC, and older Safari has no Ogg. So the format is negotiated per request:

  1. The client reports what it can play (canPlayType) in <id>_ready$formats.
  2. ffmpeg_encoders() parses ffmpeg -encoders once per binary.
  3. audio_format_candidates() keeps formats that are both encodable and playable, in order: Ogg Vorbis (libvorbis) → AAC/M4A (native aac, built into every FFmpeg) → Ogg Opus (libopus) → FLAC (native, lossless, ~25 MB) → WAV.
  4. convert_wem() tries them in order and falls through if an encode fails. tests/testthat/test-audio.R reproduces the libvorbis failure with a stand-in FFmpeg.

Sync check: a click track encoded in each format and decoded again (by FFmpeg, and by Chromium’s decodeAudioData) has every click within 0.13 ms of its original position. AAC’s encoder priming is hidden by the MP4 edit list FFmpeg writes.

Caching and serving

  • Conversion happens once per file content, cached at <cache>/<md5 of psarc>/audio.<ext>. Any cached format the browser can play is reused.
  • Output goes to a .partial file and is renamed on success, so a failed run never poisons the cache.
  • addResourcePath("rs-cache", cache_root()) lets httpuv serve the file directly; R is not involved in streaming.
  • The browser fetch()es the file into a Blob. Seeking a blob: URL never depends on the server supporting HTTP Range requests.
  • UX: the chart is rendered first. The client then reports <id>_ready, and only then does R run the slow decode (seconds per song). You can scrub and play silently meanwhile; the audio takes over at the current position.

Pre-decoding and quick-start

  • Separate process: conversions run via system2(wait = FALSE) running rs-convert.sh. R only polls the job’s status file with later, so the Shiny process never blocks.
  • Two files per job: head.<ext>, the first 30 s, as soon as it is encoded, then audio.<ext>, the whole song. Both go through per-process temp files and are renamed when complete. Encoders are tried in the negotiated order.
  • Library warm-up: at startup every song in the library folder is queued: quick-start clips for all songs first, then full files. The cache is persistent (tools::R_user_dir("RockShiny", "cache")), so this happens once per song, ever. Opt out with options(rockshiny.prewarm = FALSE).
  • Two job slots: the song you open runs in its own priority slot immediately and never waits behind warm-up.
  • In the browser: playback starts on the clip. When the full file arrives while playing, it starts muted a little ahead, is aligned by nudging its playbackRate until both elements agree within ~6 ms, then cross-faded over 80 ms and made the clock master without re-anchoring.
    • Measured: alignment 1–6 ms, largest clock step around the switch 1–3 ms, no pause.
    • If the clip runs out first, or you seek past it, playback holds at that point with a banner and resumes exactly there when the full file arrives.
  • Fallbacks: without sh or vgmstream (e.g. plain Windows) the synchronous song_audio() path is used.


Step 6 · Shiny integration

Files: R/highway_output.R, inst/highway/binding.js, inst/dropzone/

In one line: a custom output binding for the chart, one custom message type for everything else.

  • Dependencies: highwayOutput() attaches two htmlDependencys: rockshiny-core (clock.js, dds.js, shared with the karaoke player, so a page with both loads them once) and rockshiny-highway (the rest of inst/highway).
  • Rendering: renderHighway() uses createRenderFunction() and ships the chart as a pre-serialised JSON string, which the binding JSON.parses.
  • One controller per element: the binding keeps one HighwayController per element ID. A chart with the same songKey (arrangement switch) keeps the audio and playback position.
  • Control messages: highway_set_audio(), highway_settings(), highway_play(), highway_pause(), highway_seek() and highway_status() send one custom message type, dispatched by element ID. Module namespaces are handled with session$ns().
  • Drag and drop: dropzone.js turns the whole zone into a drop target and forwards the File to the Shiny fileInput inside it, via DataTransfer and a change event.
    • Shiny’s uploader, progress bar and input$file work unchanged.
    • Drops on Shiny’s own drop box are left to Shiny, to avoid a double upload.
    • shiny.maxRequestSize is raised to 512 MB (the default of 5 MB is smaller than any .psarc).


Step 7 · The renderers

Files: inst/highway/renderer.js, inst/highway/renderer-dom.js

In one line: two interchangeable backends draw the same 3-D scene for time t.

Both have the same interface (setChart(), setOptions(), resize(), draw(t, dt)) and are switchable at runtime from the sidebar or with highway_settings(session, id, list(renderer = "dom")):

Renderer How it draws
Canvas 2D (renderer.js, default) everything is painted each frame
HTML/SVG (renderer-dom.js) extends the canvas renderer’s camera and visibility logic; notes are pooled <div>s moved with compositor transforms; the board is an SVG rebuilt only when the camera moves

World space and camera

  • World space: x = frets (lane n spans [n-1, n]), y = string height, z = seconds until the note × (depth / lookahead). A pinhole camera with a fixed pitch is projected by hand (a few multiply-adds per vertex). A vertical lens shift pins the “now” line at 78 % of the screen height at any zoom.
  • Camera (_cameraTarget(), _updateCamera()):
    • it frames the union of anchor zones and fretted notes in the next ~1.5 s;
    • a dead zone means it pans only when upcoming notes come within 1 fret of the screen edge;
    • it zooms in 2-fret steps: out as soon as needed, in only when the view is 6+ frets too wide;
    • all motion goes through a critically damped spring (SmoothDamp: 0.45 s for panning, 0.8 s for zoom, 14 frets/s cap), which eases in and out with no velocity jumps.

Measured over Sultans of Swing lead at 60 fps:

before after
travel 324 frets 71 frets
peak speed 30 frets/s 6.5 frets/s
peak acceleration 1,821 frets/s² 68 frets/s²
RMS jerk 4,890 /s³ 87 /s³

Wish You Were Here went from 25 pans to none. No note due within 0.5 s is ever off-screen (checked every frame on three charts).

Ghost neck

_neckShapes() draws, in the plane just behind the strings:

  • a translucent rosewood fretboard with fret wires, nut and inlays (double at 12/24);
  • a headstock left of the nut; each string runs into its own tuning peg (six-in-line, four for bass), labelled with the string’s open note in the song’s tuning (e.g. Eb, or D for drop D).

The geometry is produced once as screen-space shapes; the canvas paints them and the DOM renderer serialises them to SVG, so both draw the same neck.

Draw order and chord names

  • Draw order: background/board/haze → beats → anchor zones → ghost neck → chord frames → sustains → gems (far to near) → chord names → strings → hit flashes → fret numbers.
  • The camera-static layers are cached while the camera rests and painted directly while it moves (a cache re-render plus blit would cost two passes).
  • Chord names appear once per chord change (or after a 2 s gap) and always on the nearest upcoming chord, outlined so notes can’t hide them.

Playing techniques

Shared geometry in the base renderer, painted by both renderers: bendAt(), noteX(), noteYOff(), forEachRibbon(), stringPolyline(), forEachEffect().

technique approaching sustain / at the strike line
bend label (“↑½”, “↑full”, “↑1½”; curves are in semitones); pre-bends ride high ribbon rises along the bend curve (full = one string gap); the string is pushed up at the fret; the glow rides on it
vibrato “~” wavy ribbon; string oscillates at the fret (5.5 Hz)
tremolo “≡” faint ribbon with bright dashes; strobing glow (12 Hz)
accent white outline, pulsing gem expanding shockwave ring on the hit
harmonic / pinch diamond outline four-point sparkle
palm mute / fret-hand mute “PM” band / “X” grey “puff” instead of the bright flash
hammer-on / pull-off / tap hollow gem + “H”/“P”/“T” normal flash
slide “↗” ribbon and glow travel to the target fret

Bend curves (<bendValues> in XML, bend arrays in SNG including the shared chordNotes records) are carried in the chart JSON (bends: {n, t, s}). XML and SNG agree point for point on all 51 arrangements (2,806 points). Where the XML bend attribute disagrees with its own curve (rounded up on some chord notes), the curve wins, as in the compiled SNG.

Rocksmith conventions

  • String colours: E red, A yellow, D blue, G orange, B green, e purple.
  • Low E on top by default (invertStrings gives tab order).
  • Open strings are bars across the anchor zone.
  • Repeated chords (highDensity) are frame only.
  • Upcoming anchor zones are highlighted along the highway.

Performance

draw(t) is a pure function of (chart, t). Visible notes come from binary searches over typed arrays, and the loop allocates nothing per frame (scratch vectors, precomputed colours, font caching). The static layer is re-rendered only when the camera moves. While the highway is hidden (the app is in karaoke mode) its loop skips drawing altogether.


Step 8 · Audio/visual sync

Files: inst/highway/clock.js, inst/highway/binding.js

In one line: a note reaches the strike line at the moment you hear it.

The chain, and what each stage handles:

  1. One time source. The <audio> element’s currentTime is the master; the chart never runs on its own timer.
  2. Per-frame extrapolation. currentTime is coarse and jittery. The clock keeps an anchor (mediaTime, perfTime) and extrapolates with the requestAnimationFrame timestamp.
    • Each fresh report is compared with the prediction. Small errors are corrected exponentially, with a 0.33 s time constant based on elapsed time, so the behaviour is the same at 60 or 20 fps.
    • If the audio runs ahead by more than 50 ms, the clock snaps forward.
    • If the audio falls behind (start-up, stall), the clock waits for it. While playing it never moves backwards (measured: 0 backward steps).
  3. Present-time prediction. A frame drawn at rAF time ts appears about one frame later, so the highway is drawn for clock.time(ts + frame).
  4. Output latency. Sound also takes time to leave the speakers. Playback is routed through a Web Audio graph, so this latency is known (AudioContext.outputLatency) and is subtracted automatically, ramped at 0.1 s/s so the notes never jump.
    • The graph is created on the first Play press (browsers require a user gesture).
    • Elements join it only while nothing is playing: a graph source starting during playback caused ~50 ms skips in the playing audio in our measurements.
    • A full file handed over mid-song joins at the next pause, seek or loop wrap; the quick-start clip never joins.
    • The last measured latency is remembered for the first half-second of the next session.
  5. Manual fine-tune. The offset slider handles anything the browser does not report (e.g. Safari has no outputLatency).
  6. Speed changes re-anchor the clock; preservesPitch keeps slow practice in tune.

Measured end to end (check_frontend.py, headless Chromium). An AudioWorklet tap on the app’s own audio path timestamps every click as it is output (getOutputTimestamp()), and the chart time on screen at that instant is compared with the note’s time:

shown minus heard
routed, no compensation +33 to +36 ms (picture leads the sound by ~the device latency)
routed, compensation on (32 ms reported) steady state −11 to −3 ms, i.e. within one frame (−16 to −9 ms on the karaoke authoring machine; see Step 13)
clock vs currentTime (1.0× / 0.75×) mean within ±2 ms


Step 9 · Song card, lyrics and practice

Files: inst/highway/overlays.js, R/vocals.R, R/mod_player.R

In one line: HTML overlays on top of the highway, shared by both renderers.

Song card and section pill

  • album art decoded from the archive’s DXT1 .dds by dds.js;
  • title, artist · album · year;
  • tags: arrangement, tuning name (“E Standard”, “Drop D”, …), capo, and difficulty when below 100 %;
  • the current section in a pill, coloured by section type.

Lyrics, as in the game

  • Syllables come from *_vocals.xml (or the vocals .sng, identical in all 13 songs of the 18-song library that have lyrics).
  • + ends a line and - joins syllables; charts without + break at pauses over 1.2 s or after 8 words.
  • The current line is shown at the top: sung syllables white, the current one in the accent colour, the next line underneath.
  • A line stays up until it has been sung, then the next one is previewed up to 1.2 s ahead.

Practice (Riff Repeater style)

  • From/To section pickers and Loop this part.
  • A lead-in with an on-screen countdown before each pass.
  • Speed plus Speed up / loop (+2/5/10 % per pass until 100 %).
  • Difficulty 0–100 %: the chart is rebuilt with each phrase at that share of its maximum level (DD charts). Playback position and audio are kept.
  • Shortcuts: double-click a section in the timeline, Practice current section, or L. All of them go through the R inputs, so the UI stays the single source of truth.
  • The client applies the speed and loop only when those settings actually change, so a running speed ramp survives unrelated setting changes.

Fixed: the lead-in countdown was computed but never shown: CountdownView reset its inline display to "", which let the stylesheet’s display: none win. It now sets "block", and check_frontend.py has a practice-loop check that asserts the countdown is on screen, the loop wraps and the speed ramps.

Transport

Play/pause and restart (to the loop start when looping), a timeline coloured by section type with hover labels and a playhead, the loop band, and speed/loop badges.


Step 10 · Input seam for scoring

Files: inst/highway/input.js

In one line: every input goes through one seam, so the renderers and the judge never know where a hit came from.

 input source ──► InputBus ──► HitJudge ──► per-note state ──► renderers
 (keyboard,        events       matches       pending/hit/       (read only)
  microphone)                   due notes     missed

Triggers

Form Meaning
controller.bus.noteHit = true “the due note was played now” (boolean form)
bus.hit({at, midi, string, fret}) rich form: the onset timestamp (performance.now()) plus the detected pitch
bus.hit({chartTime, notes}) a detector that already mapped its onset to chart time and verified exactly which notes sounded (the microphone)
bus.noteMiss = true a wrong note
highway_input(session, "highway", hit = TRUE, midi = 64) the same from R

HitJudge

  • matches a hit to the due note (or whole chord) within ±120 ms; the window is adjustable in the UI;
  • honours the pitch when one is given (so wrong notes don’t count);
  • marks passed, unplayed notes as missed, and re-arms after seeks and loop wraps;
  • keeps accuracy, streak and “perfect” (±40 ms) counts, and sends them to R as input$<id>_judge;
  • expectedAt(t) returns the due notes with their MIDI pitches (tuning and capo aware), which is what a pitch detector needs.

Renderers and sources

  • Renderers: when an input source is active, hit effects fire at the player’s actual hit time, missed notes turn grey with a red “×”, and a streak/accuracy chip appears. With no source active, every note auto-plays its effects as before.
  • Sources: register with RSHighway.registerInputSource(name, factory).
    • The factory returns {start(), stop()} (plus optional setOptions, resume) and receives {bus, judge, chart, expectedAt, chartTime, options, onLevel, onDevices, onOnsetRaw}.
    • Built in: "keyboard" (D/F/J/K, timestamped with the key event’s timeStamp, for testing) and "microphone" (Step 11).
    • Select one from R with highway_settings(session, "highway", list(inputSource = "microphone")).


Step 11 · Microphone scoring

Files: inst/highway/mic.js, inst/highway/pitch-worklet.js, R/scores.R

In one line: play along on a real guitar or bass; notes light up when you play them.

Works with a microphone, or an instrument / Real Tone cable.

 getUserMedia (no AGC / noise suppression; echo cancellation optional)
   └► AudioWorklet "rs-guitar-analyzer"     audio thread, sample-accurate times
        onsets: log-spectral flux (1024-pt, 256 hop) + level rise, adaptive threshold
        frames: 8192-sample (bass 16384) Hann spectra every 20 ms, real FFT
   └► NoteVerifier (main thread, ~0.1 ms per frame)
        "were the notes that are due now actually played?"
   └► bus.hit({chartTime, notes}) ─► HitJudge (missDelay 0.35 s for analysis)

Verification, not transcription

The chart says which pitches are due, so the verifier only has to decide whether they sound. That works for chords; blind polyphonic transcription does not, reliably.

  1. Each analysis frame is mapped to a log-frequency axis (3 bins per semitone, 35 Hz–5 kHz).
  2. The frame is explained jointly by harmonic templates for: the due pitches, their semitone neighbours (the likely wrong notes), the notes still ringing from before, and a flat noise floor. This is a KL-NMF with a fixed dictionary (40 multiplicative updates).
  3. A due pitch is present when its activation beats both neighbours by 2× (the Sensitivity slider scales this) and holds ≥ 2 % of the energy. A pitch that is an exact harmonic of another candidate and too weak to tell apart is “not checkable” and follows the rest of the chord.
  4. Rules per note:
    • picked notes need an onset within the timing window, and the spectrum must come from that attack (frame window starting within ±¼ window of the onset);
    • the verified notes must not have decayed across the attack (≥ 0.5× the level just before), so that a stray onset on ringing strings does not count;
    • hammer-ons, pull-offs and taps need no attack: the new pitch has to appear and must not have been sounding before;
    • fret-hand mutes and pinch harmonics need only the attack;
    • chords count when ≥ 50 % of their checkable notes are present.
  5. Expected pitches come from HitJudge.setChart: tuning, capo (open strings only), cent offset, natural-harmonic nodes and pre-bends.

Latency

  • Captured sound is mapped to performance.now() through the capture context’s output timestamp, minus the input latency.
  • The first estimate comes from the browser (track latency + context latency).
  • Calibrate latency plays 8 clicks through the output and matches the onsets the input hears. It works both ways: the microphone hears the speakers, or, with a cable and headphones, you strum a muted string on each click.
  • The median offset becomes the input latency, remembered per device in localStorage.

Results

  • When the last note has passed (or the song ends), a results card shows accuracy, score (100/70 points per perfect/good note × streak multiplier up to ×4), best streak, early/late counts, median timing and accuracy per section, with Play again and Practise buttons.
  • Loop passes get a short toast (“Pass 3: 82 %”) and are scored on their own.
  • The timeline shows per-section accuracy ticks while you play, and a small Perfect/Early/Late flash appears above the transport.

Persistence (R)

  • Each run arrives as input$highway_result; score_save() appends it to scores.csv and compares it with the personal best: the best complete run (≥ 90 % of the notes) at 100 % speed.
  • Loop passes and slowed-down runs are kept in the history but never count as a best.
  • R answers with highway_result_ack(), and the card shows “New personal best!”.
  • The Scoring panel lists the last runs.

Measured accuracy

tests/frontend/check_scoring.py: synthesized performances of real chart excerpts are rendered through the real worklet in an OfflineAudioContext, then replayed through the real verifier and judge. The performances are Karplus–Strong plucked strings with known mistakes: per event, 80 % correct, 10 % a semitone off, 10 % omitted, ±15 ms jitter, strummed chords and soft legato attacks. Each row is 60 s.

Excerpt Events Correct notes counted Wrong/omitted notes counted Timing error (median, p90)
Sultans of Swing, lead 110 98.9 % 4.3 % −4 ms, 6 ms
Wish You Were Here, lead (chords) 111 98.7 % 3.1 % −3 ms, 6 ms
Sultans of Swing, bass 175 98.6 % 0 % −3 ms, 6 ms
Get Lucky, lead (funk chords) 238 100 % (97.8 % before Step 12’s onset rules) 0 % (6.8 %) −4 ms, 6 ms
All My Life, rhythm (palm-muted riff) 268 98.6 % 0 % −1 ms, 5 ms
held out from all tuning:
Still Got the Blues, lead 114 100 % 0 % −3 ms, 6 ms
Riding with the King, rhythm 70 100 % 0 % −4 ms, 6 ms
  • The first three excerpts were used to design the detector. Get Lucky and All My Life were added later as held-out checks, but All My Life then drove one change (the rise threshold, for fast palm-muted re-strikes), so only the last two rows are truly unseen.
  • Live path: the same script runs Chromium’s fake capture device as “microphone” → getUserMedia → worklet → verifier → judge in real time: 97 % of correct notes counted and 0–12 % of wrong ones (1 of 8) over ~44 events.
  • The live run depends on the host keeping the capture real time. Later in the session the sandbox lost up to 0.3 s of captured audio per 8 s whenever the page was rendering; a recording probe confirmed this, and there was no loss with rendering paused. The script now measures the capture clock and reports such runs as inconclusive instead of failing.

Limitations

  • The guitars are synthetic (no real pickups, room or amp distortion).
  • Bends are not synthesized (the target pitch at the onset is checked; bend accuracy is not scored), and slides and vibrato are judged only at their onset.
  • Heavy distortion reduces accuracy.

Use headphones: through speakers, the recording’s own guitar reaches the microphone and plays the chart “perfectly” for you. Echo cancellation (a switch in the panel) reduces that but can swallow quiet notes.


Step 12 · Piano and harmonica

Files: R/instruments.R, R/midi.R, inst/highway/renderer-lanes.js, inst/highway/guide.js

In one line: any pitched part, played on a 3-D keyboard or a 10-hole harmonica.

Rocksmith archives chart only guitar and bass (plus lyrics). The other instruments therefore need a pitched source part, and the app has three:

Source Where from Notes
any guitar/bass arrangement chart_pitch_events() sounding pitches (tuning, capo on open strings, natural harmonics, pre-bends); a held bend adds its target as a second note; fret-hand mutes dropped; Dynamic Difficulty still applies
pitched lyrics “Vocals (melody)” arrangement only when the vocals carry pitches (Get Lucky in the 18-song library; the others use the “unpitched” code 254)
a MIDI file read_midi() → midi_parts() one part per track/channel (drums skipped); “Piano (all parts)” joins the piano tracks (e.g. one track per hand)

Piano (events_to_piano)

  • The exact pitches, optionally transposed by octaves (“Transpose”).
  • The left hand plays below middle C (blue) and the right hand above it (green).
  • The keyboard is drawn in whole octaves around the part’s range (at least two octaves).

Harmonica (events_to_harmonica)

A 10-hole diatonic (Richter) harp:

  1. The melody line is the top note of each chord. Runs faster than ~11 notes/s are thinned (a harmonica player cannot articulate faster), and each note ends where the next begins.
  2. harp_layout(key) lists every playable note: 20 natural blow/draw notes, 12 bends (draw 1–4 and 6, blow 8–10) and 7 overblows/overdraws. Each has a difficulty cost: natural 0, bends 1–1.8, overblows 3.
  3. harp_choose() tries all 12 harp keys (G…F#) × 7 octave shifts. It picks the lowest total cost, where unplayable notes cost 10, then prefers no transposition and the common keys. “Harmonica key” in the sidebar can force a key.
  4. harp_assign() picks, for each note, hole and breath with the cheapest technique plus the least hand movement: a Viterbi pass over the options (e.g. G4 is 2 draw or 3 blow).
  5. The tab on the blocks follows common notation: 4 blow, -4 draw, -3'' two-semitone draw bend, 6o overblow. Blow notes are blue, draw notes orange, overblows violet; bends are striped.

Examples from the library:

  • Sultans of Swing lead → C harp, one octave up, 768 notes, 4 thinned;
  • Get Lucky vocals → A harp;
  • Still Got the Blues → C harp, with 68 out-of-range notes of the solo left out (the hint in the sidebar says so).

The lane highway (renderer-lanes.js)

  • Keeps the guitar highway’s camera, clock, lookahead, beat lines, lyrics, timeline, practice loop and judge contract.
  • Strings and frets become lanes: one lane per key above a 3-D keyboard (black-key lanes narrower, between the white ones), or ten lanes above a harmonica.
  • Notes are blocks as long as the note lasts; they are consumed at the strike line, where keys go down and holes light up.
  • The camera is static and fits the instrument’s near edge to the width.
  • The static parts (lanes, idle instrument) are cached in an offscreen canvas, so a frame draws only the blocks, pressed keys and effects.
  • The DOM renderer is guitar-only; lane charts always use this canvas renderer.

MIDI files (R/midi.R)

Parsed in R like the PSARC:

  • chunks, variable-length quantities, running status, note-on velocity 0 as note-off;
  • meta events: tempo, time signature, track name, marker; SysEx is skipped; SMPTE time division is supported;
  • the tempo map becomes a vectorised tick → seconds function;
  • beats and bar numbers come from the time signatures, sections from marker or cue events (else “Part” every 8 bars).

Drop a .mid on the sidebar, or pick inst/examples/ode-to-joy-demo.mid (Ode to Joy, public domain: two piano hands and a harmonica track) from the library. The demo is written by tests/reference/make_demo_midi.py.

Guide tones (guide.js, “Audio & sync” panel)

MIDI songs have no recording, so a small Web Audio synth plays the chart:

  • timbres: a decaying additive piano, a breathy filtered-sawtooth reed, a plucked triangle for guitar;
  • notes are scheduled 0.3 s ahead at the context time that is audible when the block reaches the strike line (getOutputTimestamp), so output latency is included;
  • seeks, loops, pauses and rate changes cancel the scheduled voices.

Guide tones are on by default for MIDI songs and available for any chart.

Scoring

Works unchanged. HitJudge takes the pitches from the lane chart.

  • Harmonica notes count as legato: a breath has no pick attack, so the pitch appearing is enough (or an onset, if there is one).
  • The verifier assigns an onset to the due note nearest to it, and a repeated pitch to its later note when that note is already due.
  • These two rules came from the harmonica takes and also improved guitar (Get Lucky: 97.8 → 100 %, false accepts 6.8 → 0 %).
Excerpt (60 s, synthesized take) Correct notes counted Wrong/omitted counted
Wish You Were Here lead → piano 100 % 0 %
All My Life rhythm → piano (low chords) 99.1 % 0 %
Sultans of Swing lead → harmonica 96.8 % 5.7 %
Get Lucky vocals → harmonica 96.0 % 5.2 %
Still Got the Blues lead → harmonica 97.3 % 3.7 %
held out: Riding with the King rhythm → piano 100 % 0 %
held out: Comfortably Numb lead → harmonica 96.1 % 0 %

The piano takes model inharmonic struck strings with a hammer thump and a damper; the harmonica takes model a breathy reed with vibrato, played legato. Harmonica timing is looser (p90 30–40 ms versus 3–10 ms for piano and guitar) because a soft breath onset is placed less precisely than a pick attack.


Step 13 · Karaoke mode

Files: R/karaoke.R, R/karaoke_output.R, R/karaoke_export.R, R/mod_karaoke.R, R/audio_feed.R, inst/karaoke/, tools/karaoke_export_html.py

In one line: sing along: the lyrics light up syllable by syllable, in the app or in one offline HTML page.

karaoke

A second mode of the app, chosen in the navbar (Instrument | Karaoke), with its own sidebar, player, audio element and settings.

Which songs

  • Karaoke lists only songs with lyrics. karaoke_choices() is the library (library_choices()) filtered by song_has_lyrics().
  • A .psarc qualifies when its vocals track (the vocals XML, or the vocals SNG of official DLC, as in Step 9) has at least one real syllable.
  • The check is cached per path + modification time + size.
  • In the 4-song sample folder, 3 qualify: Into The Night has no vocals track.
  • A dropped file without lyrics is refused with a message, and the song on stage stays.

The song model

load_karaoke_song() reads only what a singer needs:

  • the lyrics, through vocals_lines() (same line rules as the highway);
  • the title, artist, album, year and length, plus the section list (Sections: name, number, start time), from the first instrument manifest (or the file name when there is no manifest);
  • the album art.

No chart is parsed, so a song opens in a fraction of a second. Its key is the file’s md5, so karaoke shares the audio cache with the highway.

Cross-links between the modes

  • The instrument sidebar offers Sing along in karaoke mode when the loaded song has lyrics.
  • The karaoke sidebar offers Play it in instrument mode for library songs.
  • Switching modes pauses the other player. Keys reach only the visible one.
  • While hidden, the highway ignores keys and skips drawing (its ResizeObserver sees 0 × 0). Both are binding.js one-liners.

JSON contract

karaoke_json(), columns as in Step 4. vocals has the highway’s lyric columns, so both front ends read lyrics the same way:

{ "format": "rockshiny-karaoke/1", "songKey": "<md5>",
  "meta": {"title": "...", "artist": "...", "album": "...", "year": "1988", "duration": 345.999},
  "vocals": {"t": [], "d": [], "w": [], "j": [], "l": []},
  "sections": {"t": [], "name": [], "label": []},
  "art": "<base64 .dds>",
  "audio": {"embed": "<script id>" | "src": "<url>", "type": "audio/ogg"} }

audio appears only in standalone pages; Shiny sends the audio separately, as for the highway.

Timing model

RSKaraoke.state(song, t) is a pure function; t is the time as heard.

What Rule
current line line k becomes current at clamp(end[k-1] - 0.05, start[k] - 0.5, start[k] - 0.05): as soon as the previous line has finished, but at most 0.5 s and at least 50 ms before its first syllable. Monotone, so the focus never steps back while the song plays.
syllable the last one that has started; its wipe progress is (t - t_s) / max(d_s, 0.08). Earlier syllables are sung, later ones not.
instrumental break a gap of at least 4 s between lines. One second after a line ends, the next line is previewed with a countdown (“Instrumental · 0:08”); the last 3 s show count-in dots. The intro works the same way.
section names Rocksmith sections are fine-grained (“Verse 1” … “Verse 11”). A label goes before a line only when the kind of section changes (Verse → Chorus), or when another kind lies between two lines (Verse, solo, Verse). A line belongs to the section that holds its midpoint: sung pick-ups start just before the boundary (Sultans’ first line starts 0.66 s before Verse 1).

View

KaraokePlayer, plain DOM:

  • One scrolling column: earlier lines above, upcoming lines below, the current line at a fixed height. It moves with a compositor transform.
  • Cheap frames: line positions are measured only on load, resize and setting changes. Per frame, at most one CSS variable changes: --p on the syllable being sung. It drives a hard-stop gradient clipped to the text (the colour wipe).
  • Two views: Stage (large lines) and Lyric sheet (the whole song, smaller). Text size, section names, count-in dots and an album-art backdrop are options.
  • Controls: click a line (or ↑/↓) to sing from there with a 1.5 s run-up; repeated ↑/↓ step on from the line jumped to, and ↑ first restarts a line that is under way. Space, ←/→ and Home work as on the highway. The timeline shows the sung lines and sections.

Sync

The chain is the highway’s (Step 8) and reuses its code:

  • SongClock: audio master, per-frame extrapolation, drawn for the frame’s display time;
  • AudioOut: output-latency compensation (ramped);
  • a manual Lyrics timing offset (+ = highlight later).

audio_feed() serves the audio the same way mod_player does: background conversion, a quick-start clip, then the full file; the browser hands over without a gap. AudioDeck in karaoke.js is the highway’s handover algorithm as a reusable class.

HTML delivery

From R: karaoke_export_html(songs, file, audio = "embed" | "files" | "none", audio_format = "auto" | "mp3" | "m4a"), or Download as HTML in the karaoke sidebar.

Without R: tools/karaoke_export_html.py — the same page, byte for byte (same template, assets, JSON and escaping; checked on all three audio modes):

python3 tools/karaoke_export_html.py SONG.psarc -o song.html            # audio embedded
python3 tools/karaoke_export_html.py --library songs -o songbook.html --audio files
python3 tools/karaoke_export_html.py SONG.psarc -o lyrics.html --audio none
#   --audio-format auto|mp3|m4a|copy   --view stage|sheet   --text-size 1.2   --title "..."
#   --cache-dir DIR | --no-cache       (default: the app's cache, R_user_dir("RockShiny", "cache"))

The Python tool decodes the audio with vgmstream-cli when it is on PATH, else with the wem2ogg package, which repackages the Wwise Vorbis stream losslessly: its output is sample-identical to vgmstream’s (0 samples offset, max difference 5 × 10⁻⁷ on Sultans of Swing). Conversions are stored in the app’s cache, so the app reuses them.

What the page contains:

  • clock.js, dds.js, karaoke.js, karaoke-page.js and the CSS, inlined;
  • the songs as JSON in a <script type="application/json"> (< escaped);
  • each song’s audio as base64 in its own <script>, decoded only when the song is opened — or a sidecar file in <file>_files/;
  • several songs make a songbook with a song picker.

The page has the sidebar’s controls (view, text size, timing in 10 ms steps or 100 ms with Shift, speed, full screen) and Load audio…, which pairs the lyrics with any local audio file. It remembers them in localStorage (timing per song). It opens from disk: file:// pages cannot fetch() files next to them, so the audio element loads sidecar files directly.

Only share pages with embedded audio when you have the rights to the recording.

karaoke as a standalone page

Measured

tests/frontend/check_karaoke.py, headless Chromium; the audio is a click at every syllable onset.

Check Result
Highlighted syllable at every syllable onset, 3 songs 720/720 (267 + 158 + 295): right line current, exactly that syllable wiping
Wipe half-way through a syllable 456/456 at 50 % (±2 %)
Focus steps back while time advances (10 ms grid, whole songs) 0
Clock vs audio.currentTime (1.0× / 0.8×) mean −0.2…+1.5 ms, never backwards
Heard vs shown (AudioWorklet tap on the output) median −16…−13 ms over 4 runs. The highway’s own check gave −16…−9 ms in the same environment, since both share the clock; this headless Chromium reports more output latency than its measured path. The heard syllable was highlighted within a frame for 24/24 clicks.
Quick-start clip → full file while playing alignment 3–6 ms, largest clock step 1–4 ms, no pause; a seek past the clip holds and resumes
Line stepping (↑/↓, line click) 1.5 s run-up; repeated presses step on (5, 6, 7, 6, 5)
Two players on one page (the app’s modes) keys reach only the visible one; the hidden highway makes 0 draws during 0.5 s of playback, then draws normally when shown (finite camera)
Cost per frame render() p95 0.1–0.4 ms. 42–59 fps with audio in headless software raster, depending on machine load; there, compositing the lyrics’ fade mask dominates (−5…10 fps), which is negligible with a GPU.
Standalone page, from disk and over HTTP embedded, sidecar and Load audio… audio play; songbook switching; settings survive a reload

With the songs’ own audio (decoded by the Python tool):

Check Result
Decoded length vs the manifest’s song length within 15 ms on all 3 songs (e.g. 346.00 vs 345.999 s)
Lyric timestamps vs the singing (vocal-band onset strength cross-correlated with the syllable onsets) best lag +40, −30, +40 ms: no systematic offset, within authoring precision
Pages with the real audio, opened from disk play, stay in sync (clock vs audio 0.1–3 ms), no errors


5. Verification

How it was verified

The original R code was written where no R was installed: each algorithm was mirrored step by step in Python (tests/reference/rockshiny_ref.py) and validated on real files; the frontend was tested in headless Chromium.

For the karaoke work, the R code was executed in webR, R 4.6 compiled to WebAssembly (tests/webr/), with the project’s own R/ files sourced unchanged. webR has base R only, so three compiled packages are replaced by small stand-ins (tests/webr/shims.R):

  • openssl: a pure-R AES-256 that passes the NIST SP 800-38A CTR and CFB vectors through crypto.R;
  • xml2: flat element lists (enough for lyrics; not the nested chart XPath);
  • jsonlite: a parser and a writer with toJSON(auto_unbox = FALSE) semantics.

A testthat stand-in runs the test files unchanged. In webR, test-karaoke.R, test-crypto.R, test-psarc.R, test-vocals-practice.R and test-scores.R pass, and so does test-midi.R except one check that compares parsed JSON integers (the jsonlite stand-in returns doubles). The chart and instrument tests need the real xml2 (nested XPath); they ran on the real R instead (below).

The Shiny modules (mod_karaoke.R, app.R) were checked for syntax, for calls to undefined functions, and for argument names against the package APIs; they reuse mod_player’s audio logic and the highway binding’s patterns.

6. Performance: Shiny page vs plain HTML, Canvas vs HTML/SVG

Question tested: would a pure-HTML frontend, with Shiny kept only as the backend, run faster? Two separate questions:

  1. Page: the highway inside the Shiny/bslib page (Bootstrap 5.3, jQuery, sidebar inputs, a text output updated at 4 Hz) vs a bare HTML page.
  2. Rendering: Canvas 2D vs the same scene built from HTML/SVG elements.

Method

tests/perf/: headless Chromium, highway fixed at 960×600 on both pages, 6 s of playback per cell, 2 repetitions averaged.

  • Normal CPU speed and 4× CPU throttling (an older laptop).
  • Two raster modes: Chromium’s default headless software raster, and its GPU pipeline on SwiftShader (an emulated GPU).
  • Cells show fps / main-thread ms per frame.

Results

chart (gems on screen) CPU plain + canvas plain + DOM Shiny + canvas Shiny + DOM
software raster
Sultans lead (≤ 32) 1× 57 / 9.5 60 / 3.9 58 / 10.1 59 / 4.9
Sultans lead 4× 32 / 29.9 56 / 12.7 33 / 28.6 49 / 15.7
Comfortably Numb rhythm (≤ 80) 1× 60 / 6.7 54 / 6.6 56 / 10.7 59 / 5.4
Comfortably Numb rhythm 4× 37 / 24.7 39 / 20.5 36 / 27.3 43 / 19.3
emulated GPU (fps only, GPU-bound)
Sultans lead 1× / 4× 9.0 / 8.3 10.7 / 9.3 8.1 / 8.5 10.8 / 7.0
Comfortably Numb rhythm 1× / 4× 12.7 / 10.4 15.1 / 10.8 12.2 / 10.2 12.9 / 9.7

Findings

  • A plain HTML page is not faster. Shiny’s UI does no per-frame work (its JS only reacts to websocket messages). Plain vs Shiny differences are inside run-to-run noise, which is ±5–10 fps in software mode; the sign flips between runs. Keep the Shiny UI.
  • HTML/SVG vs Canvas depends on the machine.
    • With software raster, the DOM version uses about half the main-thread time. It holds up much better under CPU throttling on moderately dense charts, because rasterization happens off the main thread and unchanged layers are reused.
    • On the densest chart the advantage mostly disappears (more elements to style and lay out).
    • On the emulated GPU both are GPU-bound and within noise of each other.
  • A layered-canvas variant (static board on its own <canvas>) was also measured. It showed no gain and was dropped.
  • Neither headless mode is a real GPU, so absolute numbers don’t transfer to your Mac. That’s why the app has a Benchmark renderers button: it renders the densest 3 s of the loaded chart with both renderers in your browser and shows fps, p95 frame time, % janky frames and JS draw time in the sidebar. Pick the winner in the Renderer dropdown.

Re-run

python3 -m http.server 8765                   # at the repo root
python3 tests/perf/run_bench.py 2             # add --gpu for the SwiftShader GPU path

bench.html falls back to CDN copies of Bootstrap and jQuery.

Other knobs

  • highway_settings(session, id, list(maxDpr = 1.5)) caps the canvas pixel ratio. Fill cost scales with pixels, so this is the main lever on HiDPI screens with weak GPUs (canvas renderer).
  • If neither renderer holds 60 fps on target hardware, the next step is WebGL (e.g. Three.js with instanced gem meshes) behind the same four-method interface; the clock and binding don’t change.


7. Known limitations and next steps

Audio

  • Audio decoding blocks the R process (single user: fine). For multi-user hosting, wrap song_audio() in shiny::ExtendedTask with mirai or future.
  • Background conversion needs sh (macOS/Linux; Git Bash on Windows); otherwise audio is converted synchronously on first open.
  • Output-latency compensation depends on the browser reporting outputLatency (Chrome, Firefox; not Safari) and starts after the first pause/seek when a full file arrived mid-song. The fine-tune slider covers the rest.

Highway

  • Not yet drawn: handshape durations, arpeggio frames, tone changes, left-handed mode.
  • XML vs SNG sustain differs only for chords with mixed per-string sustains (see Step 3).

Scoring

  • Microphone scoring (Step 11) is validated on synthesized guitars and a fake capture device, not yet on a real instrument, amp and room: expect to tune Sensitivity and to calibrate latency.
  • Bends, slides and vibrato are judged at their onset only.
  • Scores are per user on one machine (scores.csv); there is no multi-user profile.

Instruments and MIDI

  • Piano and harmonica parts are derived (except from MIDI): a guitar line played on piano, or a melody mapped onto a harp. They are faithful to the pitches, not idiomatic arrangements.
  • No chromatic harmonica; no sustain pedal or fingering numbers on piano.
  • MIDI songs have no recording (guide tones only). Aligning a MIDI file with a .psarc’s audio would need a time offset / tempo-map alignment step.

Lyrics and karaoke

  • Japanese lyrics (jvocals) are skipped when regular vocals exist.
  • Rocksmith lyrics are almost always unpitched (note code 254), so there is no pitch guide or singing score. Get Lucky carries pitches; a pitch lane would be the next step.
  • The recording still has the original vocal; there is no vocal reduction.
  • .kar MIDI karaoke files are not used in karaoke mode, because there is no recording to sing with.
  • A page with embedded audio weighs the song’s audio plus a third (base64), about 5–9 MB per song. Use audio = "files" for big songbooks.
  • The exported page keeps the cached format (Ogg Vorbis for most browsers). Use audio_format = "mp3" or "m4a" for older Safari.

Legal

  • Only use archives you own. The keys in crypto.R are the publicly documented community values used by the Custom Song Toolkit.
